headline: Divers explore oldest warship found off Sweden

sources.title: Divers exploring oldest warship found off Sweden find "new clues" (CBS News / AFP)
Sweden's oldest warship: Marine archaeologists document 15th-century warship Vrak 5 off Stockholm (Malay Mail / AFP)
Swedish archaelogists discover wreck of 15th century ship off Stockholm (Baird Maritime)

chunks.text: A [[warship]] more than 500 years old lies on the [[seabed]] south of Stockholm, below an old castle on the coast. Experts believe it is the oldest warship found off Sweden or Denmark. In October 2026, a team from Sweden's Museum of Wrecks {{headed out}} to the site again. They wanted to {{find out}} how the ship was built and why it sank.

verbs.why: We head out early on Saturday mornings. The fishing boats head out before sunrise. In October 2026, a team from Sweden's Museum of Wrecks headed out to the site again.

verbs.correct: To learn facts you did not know
verbs.wrong: To fix something that is broken
verbs.why: Students find out a lot on school trips. Doctors run tests to find out what is wrong. They wanted to find out how the ship was built and why it sank.

chunks.text: The wreck was first found in the late 1800s. Tests in 2025 showed that it {{goes back}} to the 1480s, or possibly the 1460s. The ship was built in an unusual way, with its [[planks]] laid [[edge to edge]], not on top of each other. The museum's [[project leader]] says it is the first known ship of this kind in Scandinavia. This method {{came about}} when ships began to carry heavy [[cannons]], because it made their [[hulls]] stronger.

verbs.correct: To be as old as a certain time
verbs.wrong: To be moved to a new museum
verbs.why: This church goes back to the 1700s. Some family recipes go back many years. Tests in 2025 showed that it goes back to the 1480s, or possibly the 1460s.

verbs.correct: To begin to happen or exist
verbs.wrong: To be paid for by a king
verbs.why: Big changes often come about slowly. Many good ideas come about by accident. This method came about when ships began to carry heavy cannons, because it made their hulls stronger.

chunks.text: The divers used special pumps to {{clear away}} mud from the wreck. Under it were bricks, a sign that they had found the ship's [[galley]], or kitchen. They also found parts of the [[rigging]], the ropes that controlled the sails. A student at the site said the [[crew]] probably ate fish, meat and [[porridge]], much of it [[boiled]]. Ordinary sailors probably {{washed their meals down}} with beer, because beer [[stayed fresh]] longer than water.

verbs.correct: To remove dirt or mud from a place
verbs.wrong: To mark the edges of a dig site
verbs.why: Workers clear away the snow every morning. After a storm, we clear away the fallen leaves. The divers used special pumps to clear away mud from the wreck.

verbs.wrong: To cook food in a big pot
verbs.why: He eats a sandwich and washes it down with milk. Many people wash their lunch down with a cup of coffee. Ordinary sailors probably washed their meals down with beer, because beer stayed fresh longer than water.

chunks.text: Nobody knows yet why the ship {{went down}}. Old [[rumors]] say a fire {{broke out}} [[on board]]. Sweden and Denmark were joined in a union then, but often fought. The project leader's [[theory]] is that the ship sank when Danish forces attacked the castle in 1501. He hopes divers will find [[traces]] of burning. The wood came from what is now Sweden, but experts cannot {{rule out}} that the ship was Danish. Each new dive helps them {{fill in}} the gaps in its story.

verbs.correct: To sink to the bottom of the sea
verbs.wrong: To be sold to another navy
verbs.why: Many ships go down in big storms. A boat with a hole in it goes down fast. Nobody knows yet why the ship went down.

verbs.wrong: To be seen from far away
verbs.why: Fires often break out in dry summer weather. Fights sometimes break out between fans after a game. Old rumors say a fire broke out on board.

verbs.correct: To say something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To write something in an official list
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a broken bone with an X-ray. The police rule out a neighbor who is at work all day. The wood came from what is now Sweden, but experts cannot rule out that the ship was Danish.

verbs.correct: To add facts or details that are missing
verbs.wrong: To clean old wood with salt water
verbs.why: Old letters often fill in the gaps in a family's history. Witnesses fill in the details for the police. Each new dive helps them fill in the gaps in its story.

mainIdea.s: Swedish divers have explored a warship from the 1400s that lies off the coast near Stockholm. They found clues about how it was built and what the crew ate, but nobody knows why it sank.
mainIdea.why: The divers found kitchen bricks and parts of the rigging. Experts still cannot say why the ship went down.

mainIdea.s: Divers in Sweden have finally learned the reason an old warship sank near a castle. Burned wood on the wreck proves that a fire started on board when Danish forces attacked in 1501.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nobody knows yet why the ship went down. The Danish attack is only one theory, and divers still hope to find traces of burning.

mainIdea.s: A museum in Stockholm has lifted a famous 1600s warship out of the sea for visitors. People can now walk on its deck and see the guns that sailors once used in big battles at sea.
mainIdea.why: This is about divers who headed out to study a 1400s wreck that is still on the seabed. They found bricks from its kitchen.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the old warship near Stockholm?
No. How old are we talking?
Really old. It {{goes back}} to the 1480s.
[[No kidding]]. And it's still on the seabed?
Yes. A team of divers {{headed out}} to it again in October.
What were they trying to {{find out}}?
How it was built, and what life on board was like.
They used pumps to {{clear away}} the mud, and under it they found bricks from the kitchen.
A kitchen on a warship? [[You'd think]] they just ate bread and cold fish.
Nope. Lots of boiled food, and the sailors {{washed it down}} with beer.
Beer with every meal? [[I'll drink to that]].
It made sense then. Beer stayed fresh longer than water.
So why did the ship {{go down}}?
Nobody knows. Old stories say a fire {{broke out}} on board. One idea is that it sank when the Danes attacked Haringe Castle in 1501.
[[The plot thickens]]. Was it even Swedish?
Nobody can say for sure. The wood is Swedish, but experts can't {{rule out}} that it was Danish.
Either way, that ship is [[a piece of history]].
